title: What the Armor Leaves Behind
subtitle: What the Armor Leaves Behind · Chapter 40 of 40
content:
By spring, Danse had become the person everyone came to when something broke.

Weapons. Pumps. Generators. Doors. Plans. Sometimes people.

He complained about the last category.

Then helped anyway.

Our workshop acquired a second bench, three mismatched chairs, a cabinet of spare parts, and a handwritten sign beneath the old DANSE lettering:

REPAIRS — FAIR TRADE — NO RAIDER DISCOUNTS.

Danse claimed I had ruined the professionalism of the establishment.

I pointed out we did not have an establishment.

He began keeping ledgers out of spite.

Life became ordinary in the way only hard-won things can.

There were still raiders.

Still radstorms.

Still Brotherhood patrols we avoided when possible.

Danse never stopped looking up when vertibirds crossed the horizon.

Some losses did not become smaller. I learned to build enough life around them that they were no longer the only shape in the room.

One afternoon a young settler arrived carrying a broken laser rifle.

Danse examined it.

“Who modified this?”

“I did.”

“That explains the damage.”

The kid looked crushed.

Danse sighed.

Then pulled out a stool.

“Sit. I’ll show you what went wrong.”

I watched from across the workshop.

His teaching voice had not changed.

“Small adjustments. Don’t force the housing. The weapon amplifies what you give it.”

I smiled.

He caught me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I do that sometimes.”

The kid looked between us, confused.

Danse shook his head.

“Ignore them.”

“Absolutely not,” I said.

The lesson continued.

That evening, after the workshop closed, Danse and I walked to the hill behind the house.

The sky was clear. Boston glowed faintly in the distance.

He carried no power armor.

No Brotherhood insignia.

Only the red scarf, a rifle, and the old holotag tucked beneath his shirt.

We sat in the grass.

“You ever want to go back?” I asked.

Danse knew what I meant.

“Yes.”

The answer did not hurt anymore.

“I miss Haylen. Rhys, even.”

“High praise.”

“I miss the structure. The sense that everything fit into something larger.”

He looked at me.

“But I wouldn’t trade this for it.”

My chest warmed.

“Even the workshop sign?”

“Especially not the workshop sign.”

“Liar.”

He smiled.

Wind moved through the grass.

After a while Danse said, “I used to think armor was what kept me alive.”

“It helped.”

“Yes.”

He looked down at his hands.

“But it also let me believe survival meant never being exposed.”

I leaned against him.

“That metaphor is finally accurate.”

He gave me a look.

“I knew you’d say that.”

“You walked into it.”

“Deliberately.”

“Sure.”

Danse took my hand.

His thumb moved across my knuckles.

“I don’t know what I am in whatever biological or philosophical sense people want to argue.”

“I know.”

“I still have days when I wake up and wonder whether every memory is false.”

“I know.”

“I still miss people who may never have existed.”

“I know.”

He looked at me.

“And you’re still here.”

“Yes.”

The same question he had asked in the bunker.

A different answer now because time had built proof around it.

Danse leaned in and kissed me.

Slow, familiar, no hesitation.

When we separated he rested his forehead against mine.

“I love you.”

“I love you too.”

No shock.

No fear that the words might be programming.

Not because the questions had vanished.

Because he had learned a life did not need to be free of questions to be real.

Below us, the workshop light glowed through the windows of the house we had rebuilt with our own hands.

Tomorrow there would be repairs waiting.

A settlement wanted help moving a generator. Someone had asked Danse to teach power armor basics. I had promised to fix the leaking western roof seam he had predicted months ago and refused to let me forget.

There would be danger again.

There always was.

But tonight there was wind, grass, warmth, and the steady pressure of his hand around mine.

Danse looked toward the horizon.

“Ad Victoriam,” he said.

I smiled.

“To victory?”

He looked back at me.

“To whatever comes next.”

I liked that better.

We stayed on the hill until the stars came out.

When the air turned cold, Danse stood and offered me his hand.

I did not need help getting up.

I took it anyway.

The young settler returned a week later with the laser rifle.

It worked perfectly.

That was not why they came back.

“I modified the capacitor like you showed me,” they told Danse.

He inspected the work.

“Cleaner solder.”

The kid stood straighter.

“And the housing?”

“Properly seated.”

Their grin could have powered half the settlement.

Danse handed the rifle back.

“Good work.”

Not outstanding.

Good.

I remembered ArcJet so clearly I could almost smell burned insulation.

The kid left, and Danse caught me staring.

“What?”

“You’ve become somebody’s terrifying mentor.”

“I am not terrifying.”

I laughed.

He crossed his arms.

“People voluntarily come here.”

“People voluntarily joined the Brotherhood too.”

“That comparison is unfair.”

“A little.”

He tried not to smile.

The workshop had grown around us almost without planning.

A rack for loaner tools.

A box where people left repair requests.

A second sign, added by the settlement children, that said DANSE'S COFFEE: ENTER AT OWN RISK.

He had attempted to remove it.

I had defended it with my life.

On the shelf beneath the main sign sat the objects that had become his history: holotag, baseball card, guitar pick, the first terrible detective novel, the folded list of things he liked.

Not a shrine.

Evidence.

One afternoon Lena came by with a radio.

“It died.”

Danse opened the back panel.

“You overloaded the power input.”

“I did not.”

“You absolutely did.”

I leaned in the doorway.

“Careful. That phrase is contagious.”

Lena looked at me.

“He does that a lot.”

“You have no idea.”

Danse ignored both of us and repaired the radio.

When it crackled back to life, music filled the workshop.

An old song.

One of the ones Danse remembered from Rivet City.

His hands stopped.

Lena noticed.

“You know it?”

“Yes.”

He looked distant for a moment.

“Someone from before?” she asked.

“Cutler.”

The name came without collapse.

“He liked this one.”

Lena nodded.

No awkward sympathy. No questions about whether Cutler had been real.

Just room for the memory.

Danse turned the radio up.

That evening we left it playing while we closed the workshop.

He swept. I stacked tools. Music drifted through the open window into the cooling air.

“Dance with me,” I said.

Danse stopped sweeping.

“No.”

“You carried home a sign from a dance studio. Fate has spoken.”

“I knew this would happen.”

“Then you had time to prepare.”

“I do not dance.”

“You did not play guitar either.”

“That remains debatable.”

I took the broom from him and set it aside.

“Three steps. We can treat them as an operational pattern.”

His eyes narrowed.

“That is manipulative.”

“Yes.”

He let me take his hands.

Danse moved like a man who had spent decades training every muscle for useful action and had never once been asked to let movement be pointless.

He stepped on my foot.

I yelped.

He immediately released me.

“I told you.”

“Again.”

“I injured you.”

“My dignity will recover.”

“I mean your foot.”

“Again.”

He sighed.

We tried again.

The second attempt was less dangerous.

By the fifth, he had the rhythm.

Of course he did.

Danse could learn anything once he accepted that learning it was allowed.

His hand settled at my back.

Mine rested on his shoulder.

We moved between the benches while the radio hissed through an old love song and the last evening light crossed the floor.

“You’re smiling,” I said.

“I know.”

That answer stopped me.

He had finally stopped treating joy like evidence he needed to deny.

I leaned closer.

Danse rested his cheek against mine.

“This is extremely inefficient,” he murmured.

“Terrible system.”

He laughed.

We finished the song.

Nothing exploded.

No order came through a radio.

No category changed beneath his feet.

The ending arrived and remained an ending.

Then another song began.

Danse looked toward the radio.

“Again?” I asked.

He pretended to consider.

“Yes.”

The next morning Rhys’ repaired porch brace failed exactly where Danse had said it would not.

I found him staring at the sagging rail.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“Your face did.”

I laughed.

We fixed it together.

That was life now: grief and jokes, repairs and arguments, Brotherhood ghosts and synth friends, bad coffee and music, danger that remained real without becoming the whole world.

Later that spring, Danse added one final line to the old list.

I saw it when he left the paper open beside the ledger.

HOME.

No question mark.

No qualification.

Just the word.

I found him outside under the repaired porch roof.

“You added something.”

He knew what I meant.

“Yes.”

“House or me?”

Danse looked around at the workshop, the road, the garden beginning badly beside the fence, then back at me.

“All of it.”

I swallowed.

“That was disgustingly romantic.”

“I’ve had practice.”

“Who taught you?”

“A highly unreliable civilian.”

I shoved his shoulder.

He caught my hand, pulled me close, and kissed me with the easy certainty he had once reserved only for orders.

Except this certainty was different.

Chosen.

Revisable.

Alive.

When we walked up the hill that evening and watched Boston glow in the distance, I thought about the first time I had seen him: sealed in power armor, voice amplified by steel, shouting instructions at strangers because someone had to make chaos obey.

The armor had never been fake.

Neither had the man inside it.

He had simply mistaken protection for identity.

What remained after he learned the difference was not softer because it was weaker.

It was softer because it no longer needed every edge sharpened to survive.

Danse squeezed my hand.

“Ready?”

“For what?”

He looked toward the house.

“Dinner.”

I stared.

“That was dramatically less profound than I expected.”

“I’m hungry.”

“Fair.”

He stood and offered his hand.

I took it.

We went home.

bridge_outro: In the Lanternweald, Danse built a little sign above the Brasswatch workshop. It named no rank, no order, and no former allegiance. Just REPAIRS, in letters he had measured twice. Greg helped hang it. Toph tested the support posts and declared them 'not embarrassing.' Iroh brought food. Danse watched our ridiculous collection of neighbors and finally took off his work gloves. 'This is a strange assignment,' he said. 'It's not an assignment,' I reminded him. He glanced at the door to the Commonwealth, then back at the square. 'I know.' His hand found mine, and he stayed to eat.
